thread.title: Torque Management: Pics of how it works
thread.first_post_html:
I had to go into work today because of an escaped prisoner. So on my way home I decided it was time to plug in AutoTAP and pull some data related to Torque Management. AutoTAP is an AWESOME program that is very customizable. So anyway, here it goes:


Have you ever wondered why your GM Truck seems to run out of power as it revs?

Have you ever wondered why your truck seems so slow after downshifting during wide open acceleration?

What happens when I hit my speed limiter on an 03-04 GM truck?

PAY CLOSE ATTENTION TO IGNITION TIMING ADVANCE

Abuse Mode
Simple Idle-Everything look great


Wide open from a stop. Timing is pulled WAY back


Still Negative Timing


Finally, A little positive timing


Peak timing of this run


Power Loss: Timing is being pulled again.


Say good bye to any positive timing just before the shift to 2nd


Positive acceleration is back



Top speed run


What is going on? Pedal is to the floor but the PCM is only allowing 50%


99MPH Limit. Foot is still stomped on the gas. Electronic throttling at its best


What it looks like at 75MPH with cruise control


There you have it. All the reasons you need to get rid of Torque Management.

Thanks guys,
I appologize for not adding this:

I compiled this data using my new 2004 2500HD, 6.0, 4.10, 4L80-E.
I have been too lazy to update my sig. I assumed since I have Electronic Throttle Control I would see the computer controlling the throttle blade in first gear. But I didn't. Either the data update through he ODB2 bus is too slow or my laptop is too slow (possible). I may do another run with only Ignition Timing Advanced to see if I can get quicker data. The next thing is I expected around -30 degrees to be pulled from a WOT run from a dead stop. Again either the bus is too slow, the laptop is too slow OR Torque Management, when used with the 4L80-E, is not as aggressive as it would be on the venerable 1/2 ton 4L60-E transmission.

I did note 2 things:

1. The data I see is not the result of change, but the PCM requesting a change. For instance, AutoTAP will show I just shifted into 2nd gear, whereas I know I am still in first. The OBD2 bus must only send what the computer is REQUESTING of the components, not if it has been done.

2. The GM OBD2 system has 2 options for Throttle Angle. The first, as you can see, is Throttle Position Angle. This is displayed in %, but is based on voltage I think from 0.1-5 Volts. This shows the exact position of the Throttle Body in the Intake. The next is Throttle Position Desired Angle. I assumed this was the accelerator pedal. However, after reviewing the posted data labeled Top Speed Run I realize this only shows what the PCM is REQUESTING the Throttle Blade to be at. I had it floored, but the PCM was showing both figures to be 58% at 94 MPH all the way to 99MPH. I see no way to display what the driver actually wants it to be at.

Airdeano, I was planning to take a ride to Thunder Racing and put the truck on the Dyno for some before after runs of the SPE Proflash. I will combine that data on another post like this showing what you are asking. Thanks man.

Well now I know why my Westers tune made all the difference in the world. No more bogginess off the line. Of course pulling timing like that will make the truck feel sluggish. When it shifts I really know it now.

IMO, TM is GM's way of preserving the life of the tranny and drivetrain (like others have stated) if the driver is a lead foot. I call the old Torque Managed pcm I had, "Grandpa Tune". Since I've had mine mostly removed, the truck is way more responsive and it only shifts hard at WOT. With normal around town driving the tranny shifts smooth like I didn't even have anything done to it.

I love it now when some guy in a Ford or Dodge comes rolling up to me and thinks he's better, but I punch it to the floor and I'm gone. It's such a great feeling when I'm doing 30 mph, punch it, downshift to 1st and the front end comes up. I can only imagine what they're thinking.

Thanks for the great info...excellent post.

Chevy rules with a Westers tune.

For the members that gotta see graphs. Take a look.
Ignore the last frame of data in each graph because that is where I stopped the graph.

Dead Stop to 4700 RPM. 1st gear-Timing falls to pieces


1st-to-2nd upshift. ~5000 RPM in 1st gear. Again Timing drops into the negative


There you have it. Total loss of HP and Torque.

post_rewrites.rewritten_content:
Today, I had to go into work due to an escaped prisoner and decided to use AutoTAP to gather data on my truck's Torque Management system. AutoTAP is a highly customizable program that provides detailed insights.

Why does your GM Truck lose power as it revs? And why is it slow after downshifting during wide open acceleration?

On an 03-04 GM truck, hitting the speed limiter shows:

- Ignition timing advance: Look great in Simple Idle mode.
- Wide open from a stop: Timing is pulled back and becomes negative.
- Positive timing peak: Power loss occurs as timing is being pulled again before shifting to second gear.
- Top speed run: Positive acceleration returns.

The issue lies in the PCM limiting throttle input, even with full pedal depression. At 75 mph with cruise control engaged, the electronic throttling is clearly visible.

This data demonstrates why Torque Management should be disabled.
A Western blot seems to be necessary.

That's incredibly impressive. The post is fantastic. It's astounding how extensively computers control modern vehicles. So, torque management can be problematic, but what are the benefits? Reduced wear and increased drivetrain longevity?
That's why they implement this practice to reduce costs on warranty work.
The timing seems to be inconsistent, which makes me curious about how my truck performs without torque management.
Thanks for the informative post!

Pull a 03-05 performance chart and monitor the throttle angle. Also, observe the dyno graph; specifically, the initial horsepower ramp will dip briefly before re-ramping upward—a common characteristic of LS1-based engines. This is a powertrain saver. Great job on collecting the data!

I compiled this data using my 2004 2500HD with 6.0, 4.10, and 4L80-E specifications. I assumed the computer would control the throttle blade in first gear due to Electronic Throttle Control, but it did not. This could be due to slow data updates via OBD2 or a slow laptop (both possible). For quicker data, I might run another test with only Ignition Timing Advanced.

I expected around -30 degrees pull from a WOT run from a dead stop. This discrepancy could also be due to slow OBD2 bus updates, slow laptop, or less aggressive Torque Management with the 4L80-E compared to the 4L60-E in half-ton trucks.

Two observations:
1. The data shown is the result of the PCM requesting changes, not necessarily the current state.
2. GM's OBD2 system has two throttle angle options: Throttle Position Angle (voltage-based %) and Throttle Position Desired Angle (what the PCM requests).

I plan to test the SPE Proflash on a dyno at Thunder Racing and provide before-and-after data in another post.

Thanks!

Understanding why my Wester tune significantly improved my truck's performance, I now realize that adjusting the timing drastically affects throttle response and off-the-line feel. While reduced torque management (TM) prolongs transmission and drivetrain life for aggressive drivers, it makes the vehicle more responsive. Since removing most of the Torque Managed PCM settings, my truck shifts smoothly at normal speeds but downshifts firmly only under wide-open-throttle conditions. The difference is noticeable; during everyday driving, the shift is seamless. I appreciate the positive feedback and agree that a Wester tune enhances a Chevrolet truck's performance, making it more enjoyable to drive.

For members interested in graphs, please review them. Ignore the last frame of data in each graph as that is where I stopped. The engine dead stops at 4,700 RPM in first gear. Timing issues occur during the first-to-second upshift around 5,000 RPM in first gear. Additionally, timing drops into negative values. This results in a total loss of horsepower and torque.

That's incredibly impressive. The post is fascinating.

Torque Management (TM) can indeed be a concern, but why do manufacturers implement it? My service technician explained that it’s primarily due to EPA regulations rather than drivetrain longevity. He stated that modern transmissions are significantly more durable than those from four years ago, suggesting that TM isn’t as critical nowadays because vehicles are built to last longer anyway.
The dealer's explanation seems incorrect. According to the graph, the timing advance begins decreasing around 3000 RPM and continues to decrease even after the transmission shifts.

I don’t fully understand why GM doesn’t focus on strengthening transmission components that often fail rather than just adding more torque converter locks every time they increase engine power. My 2004 model feels sluggish off the line, similar to an old 1985 Tempo I had in high school.

Nick99Chevy expresses frustration with General Motors for enhancing torque management instead of strengthening failing transmission components. He notes that his 2004 model feels underpowered off the line, similar to an older 1985 Tempo from high school. While he would prefer GM to improve existing transmission parts, he acknowledges that adding torque management is a cost-effective solution, despite personal reservations.
A quick question: What removes management? I've heard it can be done by wrestlers. Is that the only method?
There are numerous companies, such as Westers and Nelson, that offer custom tuning services for PROFlash programmers. You may find a local provider nearby.
Great work! I would recommend this as a sticky thread.

The graph shows that timing occurs well before peak torque is reached. Therefore, the advertised 300 HP and 360 lb-ft torque would not be visible at those points. Similarly, the 5.3 and 4.8 models would also fail to reach their peak power output.
Did you ever boot to EFI to check the TPS (Throttle Position Sensor)?
Not yet, but I see that EFILive allows prioritizing certain data items. This suggests it might display what we need. I plan to try it soon.
